The literal ruleThe literal rule requires that words of a provision of legislation are to be interpreted according to their 'natural and ordinary' meanings (Aust South Eastern Freight Lines v FCT (1943) 68 CLR 270). It is also referred to as the 'plain meaning rule', 'word-for-word rule' or 'literalness rule'. Literal rule is applied where the terms of legislation are clear and unambiguous. The golden ruleThe golden rule states that where the language used by the legislature is ambiguous, the court must interpret the legislation in such a way so as to avoid absurd outcomes or anomalous consequences (W Riches & Sons Ltd v HMRC (1935) AC 374). The mischief ruleThe mischief rule focuses on determining the mischief, harm or defect which the legislature intended to remedy, and then devising a solution that achieves this purpose. The mischief rule was developed by Lord Mansfield in the case of East India Co v Baynes (1784) 24 ER 413. The natural ruleThe natural rule states that if the literal rule produces an absurd outcome, the court may adopt an interpretation that makes common sense. The natural rule is not a separate rule but rather part of the golden rule. The common ruleThe common rule is a combination of all three rules mentioned above.
